Every AI deck looks
like every other AI deck

We've all started making slides with AI. They come out competent, identical, and painful to change. Here is the way out of that.

Dan Lenzen Director of Design & Innovation
You are looking at the alternative right now. Press → to keep going.

<section id="what-html-is">

HTML

HTML is the language of the web — the instructions every browser on earth already knows how to read. A deck written in it isn't a file that needs an app to open it. It is a page.

That is lucky for us. The web is made of HTML — millions upon millions of pages of it — and that is exactly what these models were trained on. Asking Claude to write it plays straight to what it already knows best. 

<!-- three tags, and what they do -->

<h1>Volcanoes</h1>
<p>They are <b>very</b> hot.</p>
<button>Click me</button>
what the browser draws

Volcanoes

They are very hot.

A tag is just a label. And that button on the right is a real button — go on, click it.

<section id="why">

What you get that Google Slides can't give you

01

No more dragging and resizing

You say "quote on the left, chart on the right." The browser does the arranging — on every screen, every time.

02

The whole deck is one small file

A few hundred kilobytes (plus images). Nothing to install, no account to log into.

03

Far cheaper to build and revise

Text weighs almost nothing. Rewriting a slide costs a handful of tokens, not a fresh render of the whole deck.

04

Effects that slide software simply doesn't have

Real animation, live data, a diagram that draws itself, something the audience can actually click.

05

Three different ways to edit it

Describe the change, annotate it visually, or open the file and fix the line yourself. More on that later.

<section id="outline"> how to start · 1 of 2

Write the outline first. Always.

01

How many slides, and how long you're talking

"14 slides, 25 minutes" stops it padding or cramming.

02

Who is in the room

Faculty, seventh graders and trustees need three different decks.

03

Whether it may rewrite your words

Say it plainly: polish my wording, or keep it exactly as written.

04

One line per slide, in order

Rough is fine. The order is the part that matters.

# deck brief
audience: LJCDS faculty, mixed comfort with AI
length:   14 slides, 25 minutes
tone:     plain, a little funny
my text:  polish it, but keep slide 1 verbatim
01  every AI deck looks the same
02  what HTML actually is
03  advantages over Google Slides
04  prep your outline
05  use Code, not chat
..  and so on, one line each

<section id="use-code"> how to start · 2 of 2

Use Claude Code, not the chat box

In the chat window

It hands you a file to download. Every change starts over: re-upload, re-read, new copy, new download.

Fine for a first draft. Miserable by revision four.

In Claude Code

It opens the actual file and edits the lines that need changing. It can open the deck, screenshot slide 6, and see for itself that the text is running off the edge.

Your images, fonts and sources are already sitting in the folder next to it.

+
Feed it your sources. Drop the articles, PDFs and notes into the folder and say "use these, and put a citation on every slide that draws on one." Then check the citations yourself — that part is not optional.

<section id="templates"> worth the investment · 1 of 3

Ask for a set of templates, then trash most of them

01

"Give me four different visual directions"

Keep one, throw away three. Choosing between things you can see beats describing a style you can only imagine.

02

Upload decks you already like

The single fastest way out of its default look. It will borrow the structure, not the content.

03

Upload your brand guidelines

Palette, font files, logo rules, the school-name conventions. Give it the real document, not a summary.

<section id="library"> worth the investment · 2 of 3

Hand it a front-end library, on purpose

Claude will not reach out to the internet and pull code into your deck — and that is the right instinct. So choose a library yourself, download it, and put it in the project folder.

Now it can use those styles and animations offline, and your deck still leaves as one self-contained file.

my-deck/
the project folder
  • the library you picked
  • your brand fonts and logo
  • your images and sources

<section id="skill"> worth the investment · 3 of 3

Save the whole recipe as a Skill

01

Get one deck exactly how you like it

Palette, fonts, spacing, the way slides open. Do the fiddly work once.

02

Say: "turn this into a skill I can reuse"

It writes down the rules it followed and saves them as a folder you keep.

03

Next time, just name it

Every choice you made comes along automatically. No re-explaining your brand.

<section id="edit-describe"> editing · 1 of 3

How to edit: Just say what's wrong in the chat

The fastest edit is a sentence. Name the slide, name the problem, change one thing at a time.

Vague

"Make slide 6 better."

It guesses, and you get a different deck.

Directed

"Slide 6 is too crowded. Split it in two and move the chart to the second one."

It changes what you asked for, and nothing else.

<section id="edit-annotate"> editing · 2 of 3

How to edit: point at it, in Design mode

Design mode puts the deck on a canvas you can click. Mark up the thing that is wrong, and the note stays attached to it. Or edit it directly.

→

Best for anything spatial

"This is too close to that" is far easier to draw than to describe.

→

Annotate several things, then send

Batch a page of small fixes instead of typing them one by one.

<section id="edit-file"> editing · 3 of 3

How to edit: open the file and fix the line yourself

Open the deck in any text editor — Sublime Text, VS Code, even TextEdit. Every word on every slide is in there, in plain sight. 

<!-- slide 4 -->
<h2>Write the outline first</h2>
<p>Rough is fine.</p>

Change a typo, swap a number, fix a name. Save, refresh the browser, done — no round trip through anybody's AI.

<section id="motion">

Then add motion — to your taste, and your room

Ask for the ones you want by name. All four of these are running right now.

Rise in

Content arrives in the order you say it.

Count up
1,280

A number that lands instead of just sitting there.

Type on
one idea per slide

Good for a quote, or a line of code.

Draw itself

A chart or diagram that builds as you talk.

!
Motion should point at the idea. If it is only decorating, cut it — and turn it down for a room that needs to read, not watch.

<section id="images">

Finally, upload your images and say where they go

Add the files, then be specific: which slide, how big, and what has to stay readable on top of them. Doing this last keeps the file light.

> use ColoRiver.jpg on the right of slide 13,
  put the headline bottom-left, and add a
  dark gradient behind it so the text reads

A photograph is rarely dark enough, in the correct corner, for white type. The fix is a gradient — and you have to ask for it.

no gradient

A headline that has to stay readable

White type, straight over a photograph.
